blocks.text: Upon entering he nearly fell down, for behind the door there was another step. "They do not show much consideration for the public," he said. "They show no consideration at all," said the court usher, "just look here at the waiting room." It was a long corridor, from which roughly carpentered doors led to the individual divisions of the attic. Although there was no direct admission of light, it was nevertheless not completely dark, for instead of solid plank walls facing the corridor, some divisions had mere wooden lattices reaching, to be sure, up to the ceiling, through which some light penetrated and through which one could also see individual officials as they wrote at tables or stood right at the lattice and observed the people in the corridor through the gaps. There were, probably because it was Sunday, only few people in the corridor. They made a very modest impression. At almost regular distances from one another they sat on the two rows of long wooden benches that were fitted along both sides of the corridor. All were negligently dressed, although most of them, judging by the expression of the face, the bearing, the style of beard, and many small details hardly to be determined with certainty, belonged to the higher classes. Since no coat hooks were present, they had placed their hats under the bench, probably each following the example of the other. When those who sat nearest the door caught sight of K. and the court usher, they rose in greeting; as those following saw this, they believed they had to greet as well, so that all rose as the two walked past. They never stood completely upright, their backs were bowed, their knees bent, they stood like street beggars. K. waited for the court usher, who was walking a little behind him, and said: "How humiliated they must be." "Yes," said the court usher, "they are accused men, all whom you see here are accused men." "Indeed!" said K. "Then they are my colleagues, after all." And he turned to the nearest, a tall, slender, already nearly gray-haired man. "What are you waiting for here?" K. asked politely. The unexpected address, however, confused the man, which looked all the more painful since he was evidently a man experienced in the world, who elsewhere certainly knew how to control himself and did not easily give up the superiority he had acquired over many. Here, however, he did not know how to answer so simple a question and looked toward the others, as if they were obliged to help him, and as if no one could demand an answer from him if this help failed to come. Then the court usher stepped up and said, in order to calm and encourage the man: "The gentleman here is only asking what you are waiting for. Go on and answer." The voice of the court usher, probably familiar to him, had a better effect: "I am waiting—" he began and faltered. Evidently he had chosen this beginning in order to answer the phrasing of the question quite precisely, but now could not find the continuation. Some of those waiting had approached and stood around the group; the court usher said to them: "Away, away, clear the corridor." They yielded back a little, though not as far as their former seats. Meanwhile the man questioned had collected himself and answered even with a slight smile: "A month ago I made some motions for the taking of evidence in my case and am waiting for the settlement." "You certainly seem to go to a great deal of trouble," said K. "Yes," said the man, "for it is my case." "Not everyone thinks as you do," said K., "I, e.g., am also accused, but, as surely as I hope to be saved, I have neither made a motion for the taking of evidence nor undertaken anything else of the sort either. Do you consider that necessary, then?" "I do not know precisely," said the man, again in complete uncertainty; he evidently believed K. was making a joke with him, and therefore, out of fear of making some new mistake, he would probably have liked best to repeat his former answer entirely, but before K.'s impatient gaze he said only, "as far as I am concerned, I have made motions for the taking of evidence." "You probably do not believe that I am accused," asked K. "Oh, please, certainly," said the man, and stepped a little to the side, yet in the answer there was not belief, but only fear. "So you do not believe me?" asked K. and, unconsciously prompted to do so by the humble manner of the man, took him by the arm, as if he wanted to force him to believe. He did not want to cause him pain, and had grasped him only quite lightly, yet despite this the man cried out as if K. had seized him not with two fingers, but with red-hot tongs. This ridiculous crying finally made K. weary of it; if they did not believe him that he was accused, so much the better; perhaps he even took him for a judge. And in parting he now gripped him really more firmly, pushed him back onto the bench, and walked on. "Most accused men are so sensitive," said the court usher. Behind them almost all who were waiting now gathered around the man, who had already stopped crying out, and seemed to be questioning him closely about the incident. Coming toward K. now was a warder, who was recognizable chiefly by a saber, the scabbard of which, at least judging by the color, consisted of aluminum. K. marveled at this and even reached out with his hand toward it. The warder, who had come because of the crying, asked about what had happened. The court usher sought to calm him with a few words, but the warder declared he still had to look into it himself, saluted, and walked on with very hurried, yet very short steps, probably measured by gout.
